items.prompt: Which of the following is one of the five forces in Porter's Five Forces model of industry analysis?

options.label: Employee turnover rate
Threat of new entrants
Brand awareness level
Government subsidy levels

rubric: Threat of new entrants is one of Porter's five forces.
The other options are real business factors but are not part of the model.

items.prompt: Which generic strategy aims to become the lowest-cost producer in an industry?

options.label: Focus
Diversification
Differentiation
Cost leadership

rubric: Cost leadership means having the lowest cost structure in the industry.
Differentiation is a common confusion, but it targets unique value rather than low cost.

items.prompt: In a SWOT analysis, which of the following categories describes factors outside the organization?

options.label: Opportunities
Weaknesses
Core competencies
Strengths

rubric: Opportunities and threats are the external factors in SWOT.
Strengths and weaknesses are internal, and core competencies are internal strengths.

items.prompt: In the Ansoff matrix, what is the name for selling existing products to existing markets to gain more share?

options.label: Diversification
Market penetration
Market development
Product development

rubric: Market penetration means existing products in existing markets.
Market development is a common mix-up, but it means taking existing products to new markets.

items.prompt: In the VRIO framework for assessing resources, what does the letter R stand for?

options.label: Revenue
Resilience
Rarity
Reach

rubric: VRIO stands for Value, Rarity, Imitability, Organization.
Resilience, Reach and Revenue are plausible-sounding business words that are not in the framework.

items.prompt: Which of the following are among Porter's five forces? Select all that apply.

options.label: Threat of substitute products
Corporate culture strength
Economies of scale
Bargaining power of suppliers
Bargaining power of buyers

rubric: Buyer power, supplier power and substitutes are three of the five forces.
Corporate culture and economies of scale are not forces in the model.

items.prompt: A strategy team lists the following for its firm: a patented technology, a high level of debt, rising demand in a new region, and a rival about to enter the market. The team is sorting the list into a SWOT analysis. Which item belongs under Weaknesses?

options.label: The patented technology
The rival about to enter
The high level of debt
The rising demand in the new region

rubric: Weaknesses are internal negatives, and high debt is one.
The rival is an external threat, and the demand is an external opportunity.

items.prompt: Why can a firm following a differentiation strategy often charge higher prices than rivals?

options.label: Customers see unique value in its product and will pay more
Its costs are lower than rivals' costs, so it can set prices that still cover them
Higher prices always lead to larger market share for the firm over time
Regulators allow it to set prices above the market level

rubric: Differentiation works because customers perceive unique value and pay a premium.
Lower cost is the logic of cost leadership, which is a different strategy.

items.prompt: A company makes specialised climbing shoes only for competitive bouldering athletes and ignores the wider footwear market. How is this strategy best classified?

options.label: Market penetration, because it sells one product repeatedly
Cost leadership, because small volumes keep costs low
Focus, because it serves one narrow segment in depth
Diversification, because it avoids the mass market entirely

rubric: Serving a narrow segment with tailored products is a focus strategy.
Diversification means entering new products and markets, not narrowing the target.

items.prompt: Why are high barriers to entry generally good for the profitability of firms already in an industry?

options.label: They remove the bargaining power of suppliers and buyers completely
They ensure that every firm in the industry will earn a profit
They keep out new rivals who would push prices down
They force existing firms to cut prices to keep their current customers

rubric: Barriers limit new rivals, which protects prices and margins.
Barriers do not guarantee profit or remove the other forces.

items.prompt: A manufacturer depends on one supplier for a unique component that has no substitute. What is the most likely effect on the manufacturer?

options.label: Lower input costs, because the supplier wants to keep a long-term relationship with a loyal buyer
Higher bargaining power, because the manufacturer is the supplier's main buyer and can set terms
No effect on margins, because the component's cost is already recorded in the accounts
Stronger supplier power, which can squeeze the manufacturer's margins

rubric: Few alternatives give the supplier power to raise prices and squeeze margins.
The manufacturer's dependence reduces its leverage rather than raising it.

items.prompt: What does it mean to say a competitive advantage is sustainable?

options.label: The firm promotes it in its environmental reports
Rivals cannot easily copy it, so the advantage lasts
The firm is currently more profitable than all of its rivals
The firm has used it successfully for several years

rubric: Sustainability means the advantage resists imitation.
Current profit or past success does not show that rivals cannot copy it.

items.prompt: Which of the following are likely to be hard for rivals to imitate, and so a source of lasting advantage? Select all that apply.

options.label: A brand loyalty built over decades
A widely available software tool
An exclusive long-term supply contract
A standard product sold at the market price
A patented production process

rubric: Patents, earned loyalty and exclusive contracts are protected or slow to build.
Common tools and standard products can be copied or bought by any rival.

items.prompt: A soft-drink company sells its existing cola flavours only in its home country. It now plans to sell the same drinks in three neighbouring countries. Using the Ansoff matrix, how is this growth choice best classified?

options.label: Market penetration
Market development
Product development
Diversification

rubric: Existing products in new markets is market development.
Penetration stays in existing markets, and diversification would change both product and market.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a cost leadership strategy?

options.label: Becoming the lowest-cost producer so it can still earn a profit at prices rivals struggle to match
Serving one small customer segment with a product tailored closely to the needs of that single group
Setting the lowest price on every product regardless of cost so that sales volumes rise as fast as possible
Offering unique features that let the firm charge a premium above what its rivals are able to charge

rubric: Cost leadership rests on a real cost advantage, which keeps profit positive at low prices.
Distractors confuse it with simple price-cutting, differentiation, or focus.

items.prompt: In Porter's five forces, what does strong buyer power mean for firms in an industry?

options.label: New competitors can enter the market easily, which pushes industry prices and profits downward
Suppliers can raise the price of key inputs, which reduces the profit that firms are able to keep
Customers can push prices down or demand more value, which squeezes the profit firms can earn
Customers are loyal to the brand, so firms can raise prices without losing any sales to rivals

rubric: Strong buyers bargain prices down or demand extra value, cutting industry profit.
Distractors describe brand loyalty, supplier power, or threat of entry instead.

items.prompt: Which example best illustrates a differentiation strategy?

options.label: A retailer selling only left-handed sporting equipment to a small and clearly defined group of buyers
A supplier building a factory near its biggest customer so that shipping costs per unit fall sharply
A grocer cutting prices on staple goods so that it is the cheapest store in the whole town
A laptop maker charging more for a distinctive design, build quality and support that buyers value

rubric: Differentiation creates unique value buyers will pay a premium for.
Distractors show cost leadership, cost reduction, and focus.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a barrier to entry that protects incumbent firms?

options.label: Many customers who would happily pay lower prices if some new supplier offered them
Rapid industry growth that attracts many investors who want to fund new companies in the market
Large economies of scale that give incumbents lower unit costs than small new entrants can achieve
High industry profits that signal to outsiders that the market could be worth entering soon

rubric: Scale economies force entrants to enter big or accept higher unit costs.
Distractors are incentives to enter, not obstacles.

items.prompt: Why does a resource that rivals can copy easily fail to give a lasting competitive advantage?

options.label: Copyable resources cost more to maintain than they earn, so accounting profit turns negative for the firm
Rivals can duplicate it quickly, so any extra profit it brings is competed away over time
Customers stop valuing a resource once it appears in a competitor's marketing materials and website
Regulators require firms to share any resource that more than one competitor says it needs to operate

rubric: Imitable resources let rivals erode the advantage, so it is not sustainable.
Distractors invent cost, customer, or regulatory explanations.

items.prompt: Which of the following are likely sources of a sustainable competitive advantage? Select all that apply.

options.label: A one-quarter price promotion that rivals can match immediately
Buying the same standard software package that every rival already uses
A patent on a core technology that rivals cannot legally copy
A brand reputation for reliability built over many years
A network of supplier relationships that would take rivals years to replicate

rubric: Sustainable advantages are valuable and hard to imitate: patents, reputation, relationships.
Promotions and commodity tools are easily matched.

items.prompt: A regional gym chain serves only adults over 60. It offers low-impact classes, quiet hours and staff trained in senior health, and does not try to attract younger members. Which generic strategy does this best describe?

options.label: Broad differentiation, because it tries to appeal to every age group through a wide and varied service range
Cost leadership, because it avoids spending on equipment aimed at younger and more demanding members
Focus, because it serves one narrow segment with an offering tailored specifically to that group
Stuck in the middle, because it pursues neither low cost nor any form of distinctive appeal

rubric: A narrow target segment with a tailored offer is a focus strategy.
Distractors misread the narrow scope as cost leadership, broad differentiation, or no strategy.

items.prompt: Forty small phone makers all depend on chips from just two large suppliers, with no alternative source. Which of Porter's five forces most threatens the phone makers' profits?

options.label: Threat of substitutes
Buyer power
Threat of new entrants
Supplier power

rubric: Few suppliers of a critical input give them strong pricing power.
Other forces are not the main issue in this situation.

items.prompt: A central bank raises interest rates sharply, making loans costlier for a homebuilder's customers. Under PESTEL, which factor does this best illustrate?

options.label: Economic
Social
Technological
Legal

rubric: Interest rates are an economic factor.
Other categories do not fit a rate change.

items.prompt: Firm A has a unit cost of $8 and its rival has a unit cost of $10. The rival cuts its price to $9.50 and Firm A matches it. What happens per unit?

options.label: A earns $2.50 while the rival loses $0.50
A earns $1.50 while the rival earns $0.50
A earns $1.50 while the rival loses $0.50
A earns $1.50 while the rival breaks even

rubric: Distractors misstate margins by using the wrong cost or price.

items.prompt: A bank notes that a fintech startup has just launched free money transfers aimed at the bank's customers. In a SWOT analysis, where does this belong?

options.label: Threat
Opportunity
Weakness
Strength

rubric: An external development that can take customers is a threat.
Strengths and weaknesses are internal.

items.prompt: A furniture maker wants to differentiate on durability. Using the value chain, which investment best supports that goal?

options.label: Adopting a faster delivery carrier with real-time tracking for customer orders
Expanding warehouse space so that popular designs are always in stock
Using higher-grade materials and stricter quality inspection in production
Increasing advertising spend to promote new designs in national campaigns

rubric: Durability is created in production and quality control.
Distractors are cost-cutting moves that do not build durability.

items.prompt: Which moves would apply a cost leadership strategy to a budget airline? Select all that apply.

options.label: Selling tickets directly online rather than through travel agents
Adding free premium meals and airport lounge access for all passengers
Flying to secondary airports that charge lower landing fees
Offering a personalised concierge service to every traveller
Operating a single aircraft type to cut maintenance and crew training costs

rubric: Standardisation, cheaper airports and direct sales cut cost per seat.
Meals, lounges and concierge add cost and suit differentiation.

items.prompt: A pet food brand sells dog food to existing customers nationwide. Management wants growth at the lowest risk by using only its current product and current market. Which option fits Ansoff's market penetration strategy?

options.label: Launch a new cat litter line and sell it to the brand's existing dog food customers
Launch a loyalty programme that raises how often current customers buy the brand's dog food
Buy a pet-insurance startup and sell policies to a new group of customers
Export the current dog food range to pet owners in several Asian countries

rubric: Penetration sells more of existing products to existing markets.
Distractors are product development, market development, and diversification.

items.prompt: A packaging maker sells to three large retailers that together buy 80% of its output, can easily switch to rivals, and could make the packaging themselves. Which Porter force is most intense here?

options.label: Threat of substitutes
Bargaining power of buyers
Bargaining power of suppliers
Threat of new entrants

rubric: A few concentrated buyers with low switching costs and a credible threat of backward integration give buyers strong power.
Supplier power is the common mix-up, but the maker is the supplier here.

items.prompt: A grocery chain launches a loyalty program to increase sales of its current products to shoppers in the cities it already serves. Which Ansoff growth strategy is this?

options.label: Market development
Diversification
Market penetration
Product development

rubric: Existing products sold to existing markets is market penetration.
Market development needs new markets, and product development needs new products.

items.prompt: A firm's proprietary recipe is valuable and rare, but rivals can copy it within a few months. Applying the VRIO framework, what does this resource give the firm?

options.label: Sustained competitive advantage
Temporary competitive advantage
Competitive disadvantage
Competitive parity only

rubric: A resource that is valuable and rare but easy to imitate yields only a temporary advantage.
Sustained advantage requires the resource to be costly to imitate as well.

items.prompt: A product holds 12% market share; the largest rival holds 30%. The market grows 2% a year. Using the BCG matrix (high growth means above 10%, high share means relative share above 1.0), where does the product sit?

options.label: Star
Question mark
Cash cow
Dog

rubric: Relative share is 12/30 = 0.4 (low) and growth is 2% (low), which places it in the Dog quadrant.
Cash cow and question mark each reverse one of the two dimensions.

items.prompt: A firm's unit cost falls 20% with every doubling of cumulative output (an 80% experience curve). Unit cost is 100 at 1,000 cumulative units. What is it at 4,000 cumulative units?
rubric: Two doublings give 100 x 0.8 x 0.8 = 64.
Subtracting 20 per doubling (giving 60) treats the decline as linear rather than compounding.

items.prompt: Which of the following would lower the threat of new entrants into an industry? Select all that apply.

options.label: Long-term exclusive contracts tying up key distributors
High customer loyalty to existing brands
Low capital needed to start a business
Strong economies of scale among incumbents
Open, easy access to distribution channels

rubric: Scale economies, brand loyalty and locked-up distribution are entry barriers.
Low capital needs and open channels make entry easier, so they raise the threat.

items.prompt: A regional bank with retail branches plans to start selling insurance products to small-business owners, a segment it has never served. Management wants to classify the growth move using the Ansoff matrix. Which classification and reasoning is correct?

options.label: Product development, since the bank is only adding one new item to its range
Market development, since small businesses are a new group of customers
Market penetration, since the bank already sells financial services to customers
Diversification, since both the product and the customer segment are new to the bank

rubric: New products sold to new markets is diversification.
Product development and market development each change only one dimension.

items.prompt: A software firm adds premium features and raises its price 25%. Sales drop while rivals' basic products hold share, and surveys show buyers rate the new features as unimportant. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Customers are loyal to rival brands, so it needs far larger advertising budgets before any price rise
Its costs rose above rivals', so it lost the cost advantage behind its premium price
The features were over-engineered, so the real cause is weak internal R&D productivity
The differentiation targets attributes buyers do not value, so the price premium is not justified

rubric: Differentiation only supports a premium when buyers value the attribute, and the survey shows they do not.
The other options assume causes the evidence does not support.

items.prompt: A furniture maker prices mid-range, has higher unit costs than a discount importer, and offers less design distinction than a premium designer brand. Both its margins and its share are slipping. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.label: Over-integration into manufacturing is the main cause, since fixed costs are too high
Weak market development is the main cause, since it sells in too few regions
It is stuck in the middle, with neither a cost nor a differentiation advantage
Excess supplier power is squeezing its margins and limiting its choices

rubric: Being beaten on cost by one rival and on distinctiveness by another is the stuck-in-the-middle pattern.
The other options point to causes not indicated by the facts.

items.prompt: An industry grew 25% a year with very high incumbent profits, yet five years later profits had fallen to the economy-wide average. Which analysis explains this best?

options.label: Suppliers raised input prices after demand jumped, which absorbed the profits
Low entry barriers let new firms enter and compete the excess profits away
Buyers gained power as the market matured, which forced prices down
Rapid growth itself always erodes margins, whatever the industry structure

rubric: High profits with weak barriers attract entrants whose capacity and rivalry compete returns down.
The other options name forces not supported by the facts, and growth does not always cut margins.

items.prompt: Two airlines both have low unit costs. One achieved this by buying a cheaper aircraft; the other through point-to-point routes, fast turnarounds, a single aircraft type and no meals, all reinforcing each other. Why is the second airline's advantage likely more sustainable?

options.label: Its interlocking activities must be copied together, so imitating any one gives rivals little
Its larger fleet gives it deeper economies of scale, which a rival with fewer aircraft cannot match
Its lower prices create stronger customer loyalty, so passengers rarely switch back to rivals later
Its aircraft purchase was more valuable, so rivals cannot afford to match the same deal on price

rubric: Fit among reinforcing activities makes the whole system hard to imitate, unlike a single purchase.
The other options invent scale, asset or loyalty effects that the facts do not state.

items.prompt: An analyst argues: 'Pharmaceuticals earn an average ROIC of 25%, so any firm entering will earn about 25%.' Which step in the reasoning is weakest?

options.label: Treating high supplier power as the cause of the returns, since profitable industries always have powerful suppliers
Averaging returns over several years, since only a single quarter can show an industry's true profitability
Using ROIC as the measure, since revenue growth is the only valid test of industry attractiveness
Assuming the industry average carries over to an entrant that lacks incumbents' patents and scale

rubric: Returns often come from firm-specific advantages and barriers that an entrant would lack, so the average does not carry over.
The other options misstate how industry attractiveness is measured.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest that a firm's advantage rests on cost leadership rather than differentiation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Heavy spending on brand advertising to justify premium prices
Frequent launches of distinctive, feature-rich product variants
Unit costs fall steadily as volume and scale rise
Prices at or below rivals' while still earning healthy margins
Tight overhead control and a standardized product range

rubric: Low prices with healthy margins, scale-driven cost declines and standardization with tight overheads are signs of cost leadership.
Premium branding and frequent distinctive launches are signs of differentiation.

items.prompt: A retailer bought its packaging supplier hoping to cut costs. Packaging is a commodity sold by many firms at market prices, and the supplier runs 30% below capacity. Two years on, the retailer's margins have fallen. Which explanation best fits?

options.label: Supplier power rose because the retailer now depends on a single packaging source
Integration added fixed costs and idle capacity but gave no cost edge over buying on the market
Buyer power rose because shoppers now see the retailer as a packaging company
Substitutes became a threat because integration signalled lower product quality to shoppers and pushed them to rival retailers

rubric: With a competitive commodity input, vertical integration brings no cost advantage while adding fixed costs and idle capacity.
The other options invent power or substitute effects that the facts do not support.

items.prompt: Two firms in the same packaged-food segment face identical industry forces. One has earned a return on capital of 18% for a decade and the other 4%. Which explanation best accounts for such a persistent gap?

options.label: The weaker firm sits in a less attractive industry, so it faces stronger forces than its rival does
The stronger firm holds a larger share, and share on its own guarantees lower unit costs in any industry
The stronger firm executes the same activities more efficiently, which rivals can quickly learn to match
The stronger firm has mutually reinforcing activities, so rivals cannot copy its edge piece by piece

rubric: Persistent gaps within one industry come from positioning and activity fit that is hard to imitate piecemeal.
Distractors confuse industry structure with firm differences, treat operational effectiveness as lasting, or assume share alone guarantees cost advantage.

items.prompt: A premium appliance maker spends 30% more than rivals on design, materials and service. Surveys show customers pay only 5% more than for rival products, and its margins are below the industry average. What does this analysis most directly show?

options.label: Its customers are price insensitive, so margins have fallen only because of temporary cost inflation this year
Its brand is weak, so it should cut prices to the rival level while keeping its current cost structure intact
Its differentiation costs more than customers will pay for, so the extra spend is not being recovered
It is really pursuing cost leadership, but its scale is too small to lower unit costs enough to compete

rubric: Differentiation only creates advantage when the price premium exceeds the added cost.
Distractors misread the strategy type or blame temporary factors rather than the cost-premium mismatch.

items.prompt: Air travel demand has grown steadily for 20 years, yet the average airline earns below its cost of capital. Which combination of forces best explains this?

options.label: High switching costs and strong brand loyalty keep buyers from leaving, but powerful fuel suppliers capture most of the profit
Near-identical service and high fixed costs push rivals to cut fares to fill seats, while suppliers take much of the rest
Rapid demand growth tends to attract new capacity faster than demand rises, so returns fall even where rivals differentiate well
Heavy regulation holds fares close to cost, which limits price rivalry among airlines and leaves little room to earn more

rubric: Undifferentiated product plus high fixed costs drives price rivalry, and concentrated suppliers take remaining profit.
Distractors cite forces that are not the main drivers or overgeneralise from growth or regulation.

items.prompt: A firm holds a proprietary dataset that is valuable, rare and very costly to copy. Its returns only match the industry average, because its data, product and sales teams do not share information or act on it. In VRIO terms, which element is missing?

options.label: Organization
Inimitability
Rarity
Value

rubric: The resource is valuable, rare and inimitable, but the firm is not organised to capture its value.
Distractors name elements the scenario already satisfies.

items.prompt: A logistics company buys a software vendor, claiming cross-selling to shared customers will add revenue. Analysis shows logistics buyers are operations managers, while software buyers are IT directors with separate budgets and buying cycles. What does this most undermine?

options.label: The claim that combining the two firms will lower unit costs through pooled purchasing and shared back-office functions
The claim that the deal will create revenue gains because the same accounts can be sold both offerings
The claim that the vendor is fairly valued on its standalone earnings, based on comparable software firms
The claim that the logistics company faces a growing threat from new entrants offering similar services

rubric: Different buyers, budgets and cycles mean the shared customer is nominal, so the revenue synergy is doubtful.
Distractors target claims the evidence does not touch.

items.prompt: Which findings suggest that a company's current competitive advantage is likely to erode? Select all that apply.

options.label: Its customers face high switching costs that rise the longer they use the product
Its edge depends on a technology standard that customers are beginning to abandon
Its edge rests on one visible feature that rivals can reverse-engineer within a year
Its edge comes from many interlocking activities that reinforce one another across functions

rubric: Easily copied single features and a fading standard both threaten durability.
Interlocking activities and rising switching costs protect advantage rather than erode it.

items.prompt: A specialty retailer grew revenue 25% by adding a third-party online marketplace channel. Operating margin fell from 12% to 7%. Marketplace orders carry 8 points lower gross margin and three times the return rate of stores, and they ship from store stock, pulling staff from customers. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Growth came from a channel with weaker unit economics that also strained store operations, so mix shift diluted margin
The core store business has lost its differentiation, so the margin decline mainly reflects a weakening in-store brand
Marketplace sellers are taking share from the retailer's stores, so the margin loss is mostly cannibalised store sales
Revenue growth of 25% is too fast for any retailer, so overhead has simply not yet been spread across higher sales

rubric: Lower channel margin, higher returns and fulfilment strain explain dilution through mix shift.
Distractors assume brand decline, timing of overhead or cannibalisation that the data does not show.

items.prompt: A mid-sized bank is losing small-business customers to fintech lenders. Criteria: protect the profitable core, limited capital, and reversibility within two years. Which option best meets them?

options.label: Exit small-business lending entirely, which frees capital but abandons the core and is hard to reverse
Acquire a large fintech lender outright, which fixes capability quickly but commits most capital and is hard to unwind
Pilot a partnership for the most exposed segment, keeping core pricing and ending it if results lag
Match fintech rates across all small-business loans, which defends share but erodes margin on the profitable base

rubric: A targeted partnership pilot meets all three criteria: core protected, low capital, reversible.
Distractors each break at least one criterion, through capital commitment, margin erosion or irreversibility.

items.prompt: A strategy memo states: 'We will offer the lowest prices, the highest quality, the fastest delivery and the widest range.' What is the most serious weakness of this strategy?

options.label: It lacks quantified targets, which is the main thing that separates a strategy from a wish list of aims
It makes no trade-offs, so it defines no distinct position and gives no guidance on what not to do
It focuses on customers rather than shareholders, which weakens the link between strategy and financial returns
It lists too few goals to give direction to an organisation of that size and operational complexity

rubric: Strategy means choosing a distinct position through trade-offs; claiming everything defines none.
Distractors point to number of goals, customer focus or metrics, which are secondary issues.

items.prompt: A buyer values a target at 800m standalone and expects 120m of synergies, only about half of which it controls. Board rule: do not pay away value the buyer cannot control. Which bid stance is soundest?

options.label: Bid up to 920m, since all estimated synergies belong to the buyer once the deal has closed successfully
Bid 1,000m, since paying above the synergy estimate signals confidence and deters other bidders from competing
Open near 800m and walk away above about 860m, paying only for synergies it controls
Bid 800m flat and refuse to move, because no synergy should ever be reflected in the price paid

rubric: Paying up to the controllable synergies (about 60m) keeps value with the buyer's shareholders.
Distractors overpay for uncontrolled synergies, pay above total value, or ignore synergy entirely.

items.prompt: An incumbent earns most of its profit from premium customers, while a low-cost entrant wins the bottom 20% of the market. Criteria: protect premium profit, avoid cannibalising it, and learn cheaply about the new segment. Which response is best?

options.label: Cut prices across the whole range to match the entrant, which keeps every customer but lowers margin on premium buyers too
Add the entrant's features to the premium line, which raises cost while giving premium buyers little they value
Launch a separately run low-cost offer with its own cost base, leaving premium pricing and brand intact
Ignore the entrant, since the lost customers are the least profitable and premium buyers will stay indefinitely

rubric: A separate low-cost unit defends the low end without eroding premium pricing and gives low-cost learning.
Distractors cannibalise premium profit, risk upward creep by the entrant, or add cost without value.

items.prompt: A supplier's profit depends on keeping pricing power for the next three years, and 60% of its revenue comes from one customer. Which development should it rank as the greatest strategic risk?

options.label: A one-quarter delay in a planned internal software upgrade that mainly affects back-office reporting
A rival's patent filing on a feature that only about 5% of the supplier's buyers actually use
That customer starting a dual-source programme with a lower-cost rival to gain bargaining leverage
A modest rise in raw material costs that all rivals bear equally and normally pass on to customers

rubric: Concentrated buyer power directly threatens pricing power and revenue, so it ranks first.
Distractors are minor, delayed or industry-wide issues that barely affect the stated criterion.

items.prompt: A conglomerate is evaluating diversification into a new industry. Which are sound tests of whether it should proceed? Select all that apply.

options.label: Whether senior managers are enthusiastic about the new industry and have followed its news closely
Whether the industry is attractive enough to earn returns above the cost of capital
Whether the combined business will be better off than the units would be standalone
Whether the cost of entry is low enough that a return remains after paying for it
Whether the move smooths group earnings, which shareholders value because they cannot diversify themselves

rubric: Attractiveness, cost of entry and better-off are the classic three tests for diversification.
Earnings smoothing is something shareholders can do themselves, and enthusiasm is not evidence of value.

items.prompt: A regional hotel chain must choose between a 40m loyalty and direct-booking system or 40m of renovations. Criteria: advantage lasting five years or more, hard for rivals to copy, and cutting online agency commissions that equal 20% of revenue. Rivals can renovate within a year but build customer data and loyalty slowly. Which should it choose?

options.label: The loyalty and direct-booking system, because accumulated data and habits are slow to copy and cut commissions
Split the budget equally, because half of each project still delivers some durable advantage and some commission savings
Neither, because a 20% commission is an industry norm that hotel choices cannot influence, so spend should go to dividends
Renovations, because upgraded rooms lift rate premiums at once and guests value them more than a booking system

rubric: The system meets durability, inimitability and commission criteria; renovations are quickly matched.
Distractors favour quick visible gains, hedging without criteria, or assume commissions are fixed.

items.prompt: A board proposes entering an industry because its demand is forecast to grow 25% a year. Judged by industry-structure logic, which critique is strongest?

options.label: Growth lowers profitability in every industry because new capacity always outpaces demand and wrecks pricing
Growth matters only to startups, since established firms earn returns from market share rather than structure
Growth is a reliable sign of attractiveness, but the forecast should be discounted for uncertainty over time
Growth does not set profitability; buyer power, rivalry and easy entry can still compete away the returns

rubric: Industry profitability depends on structural forces, not growth alone.
Distractors treat growth as always harmful or as a dependable signal of returns.

items.prompt: A retailer says its advantage is a leading off-the-shelf analytics platform licensed from a vendor that sells the same product to all its rivals. Using VRIO, which judgment is best?

options.label: Valuable and rare because few retailers use it well, so it gives a lasting advantage over rivals
Not valuable, because technology purchases never affect customer outcomes or the firm's cost position
Valuable but neither rare nor costly to imitate, so it yields parity unless paired with unique complements
Inimitable, because rivals would need years to replicate the vendor's own software engineering effort

rubric: Widely available resources give parity, not advantage, unless combined with firm-specific capabilities.
Distractors confuse use quality with rarity or imitability of the purchased resource.

items.prompt: A parent company owns several unrelated businesses. Which test best judges whether it should keep one of them?

options.label: Whether the business is profitable on a standalone basis this year compared with its sector peers
Whether the business is growing faster than the parent's other units in the current portfolio
Whether the parent's ownership makes the business worth more than it would be under any other owner
Whether the business reduces earnings volatility for shareholders across the portfolio's cycles

rubric: The better-ownership test asks whether the parent adds value beyond what another owner would.
Distractors use standalone profit, diversification (which shareholders can do themselves) or relative growth.

items.prompt: Porter warns firms against being 'stuck in the middle' between cost leadership and differentiation. Where does that advice most likely break down?

options.label: When a new process or technology cuts cost and raises quality together, so differentiation adds little cost
When the industry is mature and price competition squeezes margins, because any differentiation then becomes unprofitable and the firm must hold a blended position
When customers are highly price sensitive, because they reward a firm that blends low price with moderate quality over a pure cost leader
When the firm is small and lacks scale, because only large firms can afford differentiation, so a smaller firm must blend both positions

rubric: The trade-off assumption fails when innovation shifts the cost-quality frontier.
Distractors cite maturity, size or price sensitivity, which do not remove the trade-off.

items.prompt: An analyst predicts a local ride-hailing market will tip to a single platform because of network effects. Which fact most weakens that prediction?

options.label: Drivers and riders easily use several apps at once, and scale in one city does not transfer
The platform charges commissions on every trip, which lowers the earnings of drivers and the value riders get
The first entrant spent heavily on subsidies to attract early drivers, so growth required paid incentives
More drivers attract more riders, who in turn attract more drivers to the same platform over time

rubric: Multi-homing and local demand limit tipping despite network effects.
The last distractor describes a cross-side effect that supports tipping; the others are not about market structure.

items.prompt: A firm makes market share its primary strategic goal. Which are valid criticisms of that choice? Select all that apply.

options.label: High share guarantees scale economies, so chasing it can never reduce a firm's returns
Share is meaningful only for firms facing fewer than ten competitors in a given market
Share depends on how the market is defined, so a different boundary can change the number and mislead
Buying share with discounts can push returns below the cost of capital and destroy value

rubric: Share bought at a loss destroys value, and share figures depend on market definition.
Distractors invent a competitor-count rule or assume share always yields profit.

items.prompt: Your firm has high fixed costs and 80% of its customers value service over price. A smaller rival cuts prices 15% to target the price-sensitive 20% of your volume. Your goal is to protect total profit. Which response is best?

options.label: Cut prices 30% across the range to punish the rival, since a deeper cut signals resolve and deters further entry
Hold core prices and offer a limited low-price product to the exposed segment
Match the 15% cut across all products, since high fixed costs make every lost unit of volume costly to absorb
Ignore the move and hold all prices, since a smaller rival cannot sustain lower prices for long and will soon exit

rubric: Targeted response protects the core margin while defending the exposed segment.
Distractors either give away margin on loyal customers, assume exit, or escalate the price war.

items.prompt: A 40-person industrial software firm faces a dominant incumbent. Constraints: little capital, cannot match breadth, and the position must be hard to copy. Which strategy design meets all three?

options.label: Serve one vertical's workflow, tailoring product, support and pricing together so copying forces trade-offs
Offer a broad suite through many resellers and integrators, relying on their reach and technical staff to substitute for internal capability and scale
Attack the incumbent's strongest feature with heavier advertising and promotion so buyers see a superior brand in that one area
Match the incumbent's full feature list at a lower price, funding the losses through venture debt to win share quickly

rubric: A focused, mutually reinforcing activity set fits low capital and resists imitation through trade-offs.
Distractors need capital, breadth or a head-on fight the firm cannot win.

items.prompt: A strategy memo for a hotel brand lists: ultra-luxury positioning, the lowest cost per room, the widest range of services, and mass-market pricing to keep rooms full. What is the memo most clearly missing?

options.label: A larger market-share target, so scale can justify the cost position and the wide service range
A SWOT table, since listing strengths and weaknesses would resolve the conflicts between positions
A vision statement, because inspirational language would align the conflicting units behind a single goal
Explicit choices about what not to do, so activities reinforce one position instead of serving conflicting ones

rubric: Strategy requires trade-offs; the memo pursues incompatible positions.
Distractors offer tools that do not resolve the conflict in positioning.

items.prompt: A home-appliance maker with a strong brand needs about 10% growth in three years. Constraints: limited cash, no unrelated skills, and a test before large commitment. Which growth plan fits all?

options.label: Acquire a fintech lender to diversify, using the brand to attract customers, then integrate as scale arrives
Launch a new premium apparel brand as a separate unit that shares nothing with the core business
Extend the brand to adjacent kitchen products through existing channels, piloting in one region before scaling
Build owned factories in three new countries at once, to cut unit costs and open markets in parallel

rubric: Adjacent extension uses existing assets, needs little cash and allows a pilot.
Distractors need heavy capital, unrelated skills or skip testing.

items.prompt: An incumbent bank faces a low-cost app-based entrant. Constraints: protect the core business, avoid internal fights over cannibalization, and learn quickly. Which design best meets them?

options.label: Cut prices on all accounts now to match the entrant, using branch savings over time to fund the lost margin
Fold the digital offer into branch teams, so existing managers keep control, share customer data and avoid duplicated systems
Wait until the entrant proves the model at scale, then buy it at a premium to remove the threat to the core bank
Run a separate digital unit with its own costs and metrics, backed by senior sponsors and an integration rule

rubric: A protected separate unit lets the firm learn without core-business politics.
Distractors keep the old cost structure, give away margin or delay learning.

items.prompt: A software firm wants to enter a foreign market via a local partner. Constraints: protect its core algorithm, gain distribution, and limit lock-in. Which deal structure meets all three?

options.label: Form a 50/50 joint venture holding all the code, so both parties share control, split profits and commit equally to the market
License the product, keep the algorithm in the firm's hosted service, and tie time-limited exclusivity to performance
Grant perpetual exclusive rights for a large upfront payment, which removes the partner's incentive to defect or go elsewhere
Sell the source code outright for a fee, which funds expansion and leaves the firm with no ongoing obligation to the partner

rubric: Hosting the core and tying exclusivity to performance protects IP and limits lock-in.
Distractors expose the code or create permanent commitments.

items.prompt: A thin-margin grocer must answer a rival's loyalty program. Constraints: avoid a price war, lift retention, and stay within current margins. Which design elements meet them? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rewards open to every customer regardless of purchase frequency to maximise sign-ups
Tiered rewards that favor consolidating the weekly shop at one store, raising switching costs
An across-the-board 10% price cut to match the rival and signal that the grocer will not lose share
Personalised offers funded by supplier data-sharing rather than shelf price cuts

rubric: Supplier-funded offers and behavior-based tiers raise retention without a price war.
Distractors cut margin broadly or reward customers who add no retention.

items.prompt: A regional logistics firm has dense Northeast routes, strong driver training and 8% margins. Rivals bundle national coverage. The CEO wants a plan that needs no national capex, uses existing capabilities and raises margin. Which plan fits?

options.label: Cut rates to win volume from national carriers in the Northeast, spreading fixed route costs over more parcels and hoping margin follows from scale
Build national hubs financed by debt, so coverage matches rivals and removes their bundling advantage while the Northeast network funds the interest
Outsource all driving to gig workers nationwide so coverage grows without capital, trading away the training that differentiates the firm today
Sell time-definite, high-touch delivery for regulated goods like medical supplies in its dense region at a reliability premium

rubric: A premium niche uses density and training, needs no national capex and lifts margin.
Distractors need capex, trigger a price war or abandon the training capability.
